query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature oxidation and corrosive exposure, the non‐equilibrium metastable Mg‐containing lightweight high-entropy alloy decomposes to form a fine-scale, dual‐phase microstructure with Mg‐rich intermetallic precipitates that promote the formation of a continuous, protective Mg-based oxide scale. This microstructural evolution, relative to the as-cast supersaturated state, directly improves both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation performance.
generation.material_initial_state: An induction-melted MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloy designed to be below 6 g/cm³ in density, initially produced in a non-equilibrium state consisting predominantly of a single-phase supersaturated solid solution with minor secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Expose the as-cast alloy to a controlled high-temperature aging/oxidation treatment intended to trigger diffusion-driven phase decomposition, alongside parallel exposure to a standardized corrosive environment.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation: samples held in air at approximately 800°C for 10–100 hours; corrosion: exposure to a 5% NaCl salt spray environment at room temperature. A controlled comparison is made with the as-cast (baseline) samples that have not undergone aging.
generation.structural_mediator: The transition from a metastable single-phase solid solution to a bi-phasic microstructure featuring finely distributed Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Diffusional processes during high-temperature exposure cause the metastable alloy to decompose into discrete phases. The Mg-rich precipitates preferentially oxidize to form a coherent Mg-based oxide scale, which acts as a barrier to further oxidation and corrosive attack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the initial as-cast state, the aged alloy will display reduced mass gain during high-temperature oxidation (indicative of a protective oxide scale) and lower corrosion rates in salt spray tests, due to the beneficial role of the evolved microstructure.
generation.baseline: The initial non-equilibrium, supersaturated single-phase alloy produced by induction melting before any aging or thermal treatment.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to MgAlCuZnGd high-entropy alloys and similar lightweight systems (density <6 g/cm³) under conditions that promote microstructural evolution through high-temperature oxidation (around 800°C) and standard corrosion environments (e.g., salt spray).
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the phase decomposition and scale formation, as well as the impact of minor compositional variations on the protective film’s integrity, remain to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one in the as-cast, non-equilibrium state and another subjected to high-temperature aging (e.g., 800°C for 50 hours) to induce microstructural evolution. Characterize both sets using XRD (for phase identification), SEM/TEM (for microstructural analysis), and XPS (for surface oxide composition). Subsequently, perform high-temperature oxidation tests (tracking weight gain in air at 800°C) and corrosion tests (using salt spray and electrochemical measurements such as EIS).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show the expected formation of fine, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates or a continuous Mg-based oxide scale—and if there is no statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance and corrosion behavior compared to the as-cast state—the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
